extracted.subtask_description: Standards and tests for allowing or denying amendments and re-issue of U.S. patents (when re-issue may correct defects, and when it is barred by fraud, intent, abandonment, prosecution history, or delay). Focuses on whether omissions/limitations were inadvertent, intentional, or fraudulent and on consequences of prosecution conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification sufficiency presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The law presumes that every one who applies for a patent will embody his invention in specifications sufficiently definite to preserve as much of his discovery as he desires to protect by a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If, from mistake, he has overlooked anything within the scope of his invention, he may surrender his patent on that ground and claim a new one in accordance with amended specifications; but relief will be denied unless brought within the statute, and not if omission resulted from culpable negligence or misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue to correct inadvertence only
rubrics_metrics.description: An error which occurs through inadvertence, accident, or mistake is neither intentional nor fraudulent, and amendment by re-issue is permitted for correcting this kind of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue is for correcting honest mistakes so the patent describes the invention as the inventor conceived it and rendered it available for public use. See contrast with intentional or fraudulent omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: No re-issue for fraud-induced defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-issue is not permitted where the defects or insufficiencies in the description or claims arose through fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a fraudulent, deceptive intention existed is a question of fact; the Commissioner may inquire into original good faith and deny re-issue upon satisfactory proof of bad faith; courts may treat a re-issue as invalid if fraudulent intent appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence and good faith required for re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to amend a defective patent either by disclaimer or re-issue is conditioned upon the absence of any fraudulent or deceptive intention; diligence and good faith are required of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee must show good faith and absence of corruption in applying for a re-issue; see cases such as Miller v. Brass Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot claim matter intentionally omitted or intentionally included
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot claim matter intentionally omitted from the original, nor can it be used to restore matter intentionally excluded from the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter deliberately embraced within or excluded from a patent cannot be reclaimed by amendment; the central difficulty is determining whether the original misstatement was deliberate or unintentional, using surrounding circumstances (face of patent, PTO records, inventor's conduct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent to abandon shown by express disclaimer or conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A voluntary and intelligent disavowal (express disclaimer) in the original patent or during prosecution is conclusive evidence of intentional exclusion of matter from the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer in the specification or filed subsequently, or withdrawal of claims by amendment (to save application or escape interference), or acquiescence in examiner's rejection can indicate intentional abandonment; such matter generally cannot be reclaimed by re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel and abandonment judged by conduct and circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment is a question of intention to be gathered from the conduct of the inventor; estoppel rests upon an actual or presumed intention of the inventor and is effective to forbid departure from positions once assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumstances may precede, be concurrent with, or follow issue; they may appear on the face of the patent, in PTO records, or in inventor actions; these determine whether errors were deliberate or unintentional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot enlarge claims to include matter once intentionally excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue is not permitted to enlarge the claims of the original patent by including matter once intentionally excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efforts to extend claims that encroach on domain left open to the public or occupied by rivals are subject to strict scrutiny; attempts to claim subordinate inventions described but not claimed are particularly vulnerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations imposed during prosecution are binding when accepted
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations and disclaimers imposed by the Patent Office which narrow the scope of the invention as described and claimed in the application are irrevocable admissions that such limitations are of the essence of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a patentee accepts his patent containing such limitations, he is bound by them even if they were voluntary or enforced; third parties rely on these limitations. A disclaimer directed by the Commissioner in an application for a re-issue does not necessarily concede that the modification was not covered in the original patent (case-specific).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence in examiner's rejection bars later re-instatement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim rejected by the Patent Office and whose rejection the applicant acquiesced in cannot later be re-inserted by re-issue (no accident, inadvertence, or mistake to justify re-issue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include when a claim was erased/withdrawn to obtain allowance of other claims; acceptance of the residue and issue with such erasures estops the patentee from later reasserting the erased claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of claims to avoid interference is final
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim withdrawn from the application to escape an interference cannot be included later in a re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawn claims to secure issue are considered finally repudiated. See Ex parte Cobb, Leggett v. Avery, and related authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims formally abandoned in PTO cannot be reclaimed
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter abandoned in the Patent Office cannot be reclaimed by re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant or his attorney caused erasure/withdrawal or acquiesced in rejections, later attempts to re-claim that matter in a re-issue are usually barred; courts express disapproval of attempts to get re-issues that reverse prior PTO decisions to the prejudice of the public or rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue addresses the application, not the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Inadvertence, etc.’ exists in reference to the application, not the invention, and occurs only where the former does not describe and claim what the inventor intended to protect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is whether the omission was from the application/specification/claims rather than a change in the inventor’s view of patentability or strategy; errors of opinion or judgment are not 'mistake or inadvertence'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreasonable delay can bar re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue that seeks to restore matter omitted from the original claims is barred unless the claims are amended by re-issue without unreasonable delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less delay is allowable when narrowing claims than when expanding them, but unreasonable delay or intervening rights acquired by others can preclude re-issue. Cases: Ex parte Mathews; Ives v. Salant; examples shown where delay defeated relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue sometimes allowed to cure description even if claim-right lost by delay
rubrics_metrics.description: A defect in the Description may be cured by re-issue even though the right to cure a defect in a Claim has been lost by delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts sometimes permit amendments that place the public in fuller possession without enlarging inventor's privileges; balancing public interest vs. rights of others is required (e.g., Miller v. Brass Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney-made disclaimers and erasures: effect varies
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer by an attorney without authority may not always bar re-issue; conversely, an erasure by an attorney of a rejected claim may indicate lack of inadvertence and be evidence against re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material matters generally cannot be disclaimed by an attorney of his own motion; an unauthorized disclaimer may not bind the patentee, but certain acts by counsel (acceptance, erasure) have been held to constitute abandonment. Courts differ on some points (see Ex parte Hatchman and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims stricken in interference cannot be restored in re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims cannot be restored after a judgment in an interference has struck them out in favor of another party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once rights are adjudicated in an interference, the patentee cannot later claim in re-issue what was awarded to the opponent.

rubrics_metrics.name: A re-issue cannot be procured to cover matter once disclaimed by the original inventor (by assignment exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue upon the application of an assignee cannot cover matter once disclaimed by the original inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfers and assignments do not permit an assignee to reclaim matter disclaimed by the inventor in the original application or patent (cases cited: Putnam v. Hutchinson; others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of patent containing narrower claims estops asserting broader invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee accepts a patent containing limitations which narrow the scope of his invention, he is bound by those limitations and if he accepts a claim not covering his entire invention he abandons the residue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the limitation was enforced by PTO rather than voluntarily assumed, acceptance of the resulting patent may prevent later enlargement by re-issue. See Toepfer v. Goetz and related authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot be used to secure claims that another subsequently obtained
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim abandoned in the original application on an objection by the Patent Office, but afterward allowed to another applicant, may be inserted in the re-issue only in limited circumstances; generally re-issue cannot appropriate rights others have obtained in the interim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly disfavored where intervening rights have vested; courts protect third-party reliance and public domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue not available to correct mistakes of opinion or judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: An error in opinion or judgment is not 'mistake or inadvertence' and does not justify re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an inventor or counsel intentionally decided not to claim certain subject matter because of perceived non-patentability or strategy, that is not the kind of inadvertence re-issue is meant to correct (see Ex parte Mahnken).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's decision on good faith is final except by repeal proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision of the Commissioner on the good faith of the patentee in applying for a re-issue is final, except upon proceedings brought to repeal the re-issued patent; courts may nevertheless inquire into fraud in suits on the re-issued patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Commissioner has primary authority to deny re-issue for bad faith, courts retain power to invalidate re-issues where fraud is shown on collateral attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may reinstate claims omitted by misunderstanding of attorney if timely
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue may embrace a claim shown in the original application and erased by a misunderstanding of the attorney, provided the re-issue is sought without unreasonable delay and other bars do not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an exception: mistakes by counsel in drafting that are not attributable to the inventor personally may sometimes be corrected, but material matters generally require applicant's action; see Stutz v. Armstrong.
